questions.prompt: During an arrest, a trained responder finds that the replacement defibrillator has unfamiliar controls. What preparedness issue does this reveal?
options: Device-specific competent response readiness was incomplete.
All defibrillators are interchangeable without user preparation.
A previous BLS certificate establishes every device operation skill.
Only the physical location of the defibrillator matters.
questions.explanation: Emergency readiness includes knowing the available device's function within the assigned role, not only general credentials or location.
whyOthers: Differences in controls can matter under time pressure.
General training does not establish familiarity with every model.
Location enables access but not competent operation.

questions.prompt: A pandemic plan allocated rooms using last week's case load, but demand and available staff have changed. What is the best leadership response?
options: Update coordinated operations using current clinical capacity.
Keep the allocation unchanged so the written plan remains consistent.
Let each room independently change its staffing and priority rules.
Revise supply estimates while leaving clinical capacity unexamined.
questions.explanation: A pandemic response adapts to evolving clinical and resource conditions through consistent coordination.
whyOthers: Consistency of an outdated plan is not current safety.
Uncoordinated changes can create conflicts.
Supplies are only one part of service capacity.

questions.prompt: A patient screened positive under the pandemic definition is awaiting confirmation. A negative result is expected, but urgent care is needed now. Which pathway is appropriate?
options: The designated suspected-positive pathway until status and risk are clarified.
The routine pathway because the expected result is negative.
Automatic cohorting with confirmed-positive patients.
No precautions because the patient has not yet been diagnosed.
questions.explanation: Current screening and risk determine interim routing; expectations do not substitute for clarified status.
whyOthers: An anticipated result does not establish present risk.
Suspected status does not automatically justify confirmed-positive cohorting.
Additional precautions can begin before confirmation.

questions.prompt: A surgical delay decision is clinically justified during a surge, but the patient receives only a new appointment date. What communication is missing?
options: The individualized rationale, potential consequences, and follow-up plan for the delay.
A general description of scheduling pressure and the unit’s revised capacity.
A general assurance of fairness and the names of scheduling decision makers.
A general explanation that original dates may change during a pandemic.
questions.explanation: Transparent deferral communication includes the individual's risks and plan, not merely logistics or reassurance.
whyOthers: Service pressures do not explain the patient’s individualized rationale and consequences of delay.
Fairness statements alone do not communicate patient-specific risks and follow-up.
An explanation of possible date changes does not address the individual clinical tradeoff.

questions.prompt: After the suspected pandemic case, staff propose discarding a reusable instrument rather than using its validated pathway, despite no disease-specific requirement to discard it. What is the best approach?
options: Validated processing with the indicated risk controls.
Use routine processing but omit risk communication because the device is reusable.
Extend sterilization while reducing cleaning to shorten turnaround.
Discard the device because suspected infection prevents every reuse pathway.
questions.explanation: Pandemic risk modifies indicated precautions and routing while preserving validated device-processing requirements.
whyOthers: A validated pathway still requires indicated precautions and risk communication.
A longer sterilization exposure does not replace required cleaning.
Suspected infection does not invalidate an otherwise applicable validated pathway without a disease-specific restriction.

questions.prompt: Two disposable devices perform similarly, but one has unreliable delivery and substantial special-storage requirements. What should procurement compare?
options: The full safe-use and supply pathway.
Compare acquisition price and leave processing costs to another budget.
Compare performance and leave stock reliability to the supplier.
Compare delivery speed and leave storage feasibility until implementation.
questions.explanation: Supply continuity, storage, training, disposal, and safety can change the value and feasibility of a disposable device.
whyOthers: Budget separation does not remove processing from the actual safe-use pathway.
Performance alone does not establish reliable availability for care.
Delivery timing alone does not establish that local storage requirements can be met.

questions.prompt: A current user guide exists on a vendor portal that staff cannot access during a network outage. What support change is most useful?
options: Provide a reliable accessible current instruction pathway for point-of-care use.
Rely on the vendor portal regardless of local accessibility.
Print an obsolete guide because any written instruction is sufficient.
Remove instructions because staff were previously trained.
questions.explanation: Instructions must be current and readily accessible, including when troubleshooting requires them.
whyOthers: Existence elsewhere does not establish usable access.
Obsolete directions may conflict with the current device.
Training and accessible reference serve complementary purposes.

questions.prompt: A maintenance sticker shows a recent date, but the underlying record does not identify the device or checks performed. What remains uncertain?
options: Device-specific maintenance identity and actions are unverified.
The record is complete if the sticker follows the local colour convention.
The record is complete if users recall a successful case that day.
The record is complete if the purchasing invoice identifies the device.
questions.explanation: Useful records link device identity, checks, findings, and corrective actions; a date alone is not that evidence.
whyOthers: Sticker format does not identify which maintenance actions were completed on the device.
Successful use is not a substitute for device-specific maintenance documentation.
Purchase identity does not establish the subsequent checks performed.

questions.prompt: A serial-number recall arrives after affected devices may have been used. Which capability best supports both stock control and follow-up?
options: Trace affected device identity, location, and relevant clinical-use history.
Trace unopened stock quantities and infer prior use from the purchase total.
Trace device brand names and infer serial identity from visual appearance.
Trace reported malfunctions and follow up only devices linked to a complaint.
questions.explanation: Targeted recall response needs specific traceability rather than aggregate inventory or recollection.
whyOthers: Inventory arithmetic does not reliably identify individual affected devices and patients.
Brand and appearance do not establish the serial-number applicability of the recall.
A recall can apply before any clinical malfunction is reported.

questions.prompt: The failed device's backup is a different model with compatible intended use, but the available operator does not know its alarm controls. What must be resolved before relying on it?
options: Verified function and competent operation of the replacement.
A successful power-on check without checking operator alarm competence.
Operator familiarity with the old model without checking the replacement.
A compatible intended use without checking the connected system’s function.
questions.explanation: A backup is safe only when the replacement system and its use are ready; a newer functional model can still be unfamiliar.
whyOthers: Device function and competent clinical operation are separate readiness conditions.
Experience with one model does not verify competence or function of another.
An appropriate indication does not prove the actual connected setup works safely.

questions.prompt: During a pandemic, clinical staff remain available but environmental services and laundry support are disrupted. What should staffing planning account for?
options: Essential support services as well as clinical coverage.
Nursing coverage, with cleaning and laundry absorbed without assessing capacity.
Open-room capacity, with support demand assumed to fall as volume rises.
Surgeon coverage, with essential support reviewed only after a cancellation.
questions.explanation: Safe surgical capacity depends on cleaning, linen, and other essential support roles, not just direct clinical headcount.
whyOthers: Support-service capacity and competence need explicit planning, not unassessed absorption.
Room availability does not establish adequate support to operate it safely.
Reactive review after failure does not support continuity of essential services.

questions.prompt: A supplier substitutes a different respirator model during a shortage. The product is approved, but local users were fit-tested to the former model. What must be resolved?
options: The new model's required individual fit and preparation.
Confirm equivalent filtration and use the prior model’s fit-test result.
Confirm a satisfactory seal check and use it as the new fit-test result.
Confirm the supplier’s approval and use it as individual fit evidence.
questions.explanation: Approved protection still requires the model-specific fit and use conditions for the actual wearer.
whyOthers: A filtration category does not establish person-specific fit of a different model.
A user seal check does not replace model-specific fit testing when required.
Product approval does not establish fit for the individual wearer.

questions.prompt: A new isolation workflow is published, but staff continue mixing steps from the old and new versions. What intervention best tests reliable uptake?
options: Evaluate supported practice of the approved workflow.
Collect signatures confirming the document was opened.
Count poster copies displayed in the corridor.
Ask each shift to create its own hybrid sequence.
questions.explanation: Implementation requires observed consistent application; receipt of information does not establish performance.
whyOthers: Document access does not prove correct execution.
Display counts measure availability rather than practice.
Hybrid local variants may defeat the approved control sequence.

questions.prompt: A scrubbed team member sits during a procedure and then stands, exposing gown areas previously below the field level. What concern should be assessed?
options: The change can bring previously nonsterile gown areas into the working zone.
Maintaining glove height alone establishes safe transition back to standing.
An initially sterile gown establishes sterility after any height change.
Cleaning the chair establishes sterility of all gown areas during standing.
questions.explanation: Sterile boundaries are spatial; changing levels can expose areas that were outside the prior sterile field.
whyOthers: Glove position does not verify that other gown surfaces stayed within sterile boundaries.
Initial processing does not make every gown surface sterile throughout use.
A clean chair does not redefine the sterile gown working boundaries.

questions.prompt: For the head-and-neck case, prep drying is complete but oxygen can accumulate under drapes near the energy site. Which remaining issue has priority before activation?
options: Resolve oxygen-related enrichment in the shared fire plan.
Treat dry preparation as proof the whole fire triangle is controlled.
Focus only on the return electrode location.
Proceed because the electrosurgical pencil will be used briefly.
questions.explanation: Removing liquid fuel does not remove oxidizer enrichment or ignition risk; fire prevention integrates all elements.
whyOthers: One controlled element does not establish the entire risk plan.
Electrode safety is important but does not resolve airway oxidizer enrichment.
Brief activation can still supply an ignition source.

questions.prompt: After turning a patient prone, the airway is secure but a support compresses a dependent area and a line is under tension. Which assessment is most appropriate?
options: Correct the line and loading risks collaboratively.
Accept the position because airway security is the decisive endpoint.
Correct the line only and defer pressure assessment until emergence.
Wait for a physiologic alarm before changing the supports.
questions.explanation: Post-turn verification includes airway, lines, tissue protection, alignment, and tolerance; one passing check does not establish safety.
whyOthers: Airway access is necessary but not sufficient.
Both identified hazards require timely correction.
A mechanical injury risk may exist before an alarm.

questions.prompt: After prolonged lithotomy, one team member begins lowering a leg while the other leg remains elevated. What is the best response?
options: Coordinate controlled simultaneous lowering with the anesthesia provider and team.
Continue because lowering one leg reduces the load sooner.
Lower the other leg rapidly to catch up.
Keep the elevated leg up until the first leg reaches the table.
questions.explanation: Lithotomy transitions need coordinated handling and reassessment to avoid asymmetric mechanical and physiologic stress.
whyOthers: Unilateral movement can create avoidable asymmetry.
Rushed correction adds uncoordinated movement.
Staged asymmetric lowering preserves the problem.

questions.prompt: A high-risk patient has a pressure-redistributing surface, but a rigid accessory creates concentrated pressure. What remains necessary?
options: Reassess and correct accessory pressure despite the protective support surface.
Use the support-surface specification to clear every accessory contact.
Use the initial skin assessment to clear the accessory for the entire case.
Use normal physiologic monitors to defer device-contact assessment.
questions.explanation: The support surface complements individualized positioning and device assessment; it cannot neutralize every local pressure source.
whyOthers: The surface cannot be assumed to neutralize focal loading from a rigid accessory.
An initial skin assessment does not remove the need to assess later device pressure.
Routine physiologic stability does not exclude local pressure injury.

questions.prompt: The final count is reported correct, but a detachable item is credibly suspected missing. What should the team do?
options: Investigate the specific concern through the retained-item prevention process.
Dismiss it because a correct count excludes retention.
Repeat only the spoken total without inspecting the item.
Classify the concern as a paperwork issue and defer it.
questions.explanation: A recorded correct count is not infallible; credible contradictory evidence requires investigation.
whyOthers: Counts can contain omissions or errors.
Repeating a number does not resolve a specific missing component.
Potential retention is a current patient-safety concern.

questions.prompt: After the closing sponge count, another package is opened for continued wound work. What is required before count completion?
options: Verify and record the addition and reconcile every added sponge.
Retain the earlier total because the closing count was already announced.
Track only the sponges actually placed in the wound.
Count the package label without viewing its contents.
questions.explanation: The count remains accountable for items introduced throughout the procedure; additions need actual verification and documentation.
whyOthers: A new addition changes the inventory.
Field items can be lost even if wound use was not recognized.
Expected package quantity does not replace observed counting.

questions.prompt: An instrument has a detachable tip. The handle is counted back, but the tip's presence is not verified. What prevents accepting the instrument as fully accounted for?
options: Verify the detachable tip before accepting the instrument as complete.
Use the returned handle’s identity to account for the whole instrument.
Use the original tray list to account for the detached component.
Use the component’s small size to exclude it from reconciliation.
questions.explanation: Detachable components can be retained; instrument accountability includes verifying relevant parts, not just the main body.
whyOthers: Returning the handle does not prove the detachable tip is present.
Expected inventory does not replace verification of actual component completeness.
Small detachable parts remain relevant to retained-item prevention.

questions.prompt: The abdominal case's missing item is not found on the sterile field. Environmental search and methodical wound examination have not occurred. What should the team do next?
options: Continue the structured search and escalation process while preserving the unresolved count status.
Accept the count because the sterile field has been searched.
Skip every remaining step and label the item outside the patient by assumption.
Finish closure and report only the negative field search.
questions.explanation: One negative search does not complete the defined discrepancy response or establish the item's location.
whyOthers: Other locations remain unexamined.
An unsupported location assumption cannot reconcile the item.
Closure and incomplete reporting can bypass required investigation.

questions.prompt: The tourniquet cuff appears intact, but pressure readings fluctuate implausibly during its pre-use test. What is the best decision?
options: Resolve the unreliable pressure function before accepting tourniquet readiness.
Accept the cuff inspection as the decisive readiness test.
Accept the average displayed pressure as the intended setting.
Accept the surgeon’s usual pressure as compensation for the display.
questions.explanation: The system needs reliable pressure function as well as intact components; an unstable test requires correction.
whyOthers: A sound cuff does not establish that the pressure system functions reliably.
Averaging implausible readings does not validate actual controlled pressure.
A usual requested setting does not establish that unreliable equipment delivers it.

questions.prompt: Two similar syringes are transferred to the field with labels, but the receiving scrub nurse did not visually verify them with the circulator. What remains missing?
options: Complete the shared visual and verbal medication verification.
Use correct syringe labels as the endpoint of the transfer check.
Use a later medication chart entry as the endpoint of verification.
Use the surgeon’s recognition of the syringe as the endpoint.
questions.explanation: Labelling and shared verification are complementary controls in the medication transfer process.
whyOthers: Labels are essential but do not replace the specified shared verification.
Documentation after transfer does not complete the required current check.
Recognition by another person does not replace sender-receiver verification.

questions.prompt: An insufflator alarms while the patient's physiology also changes. What should guide the immediate team response?
options: Assess the patient’s change together with the insufflation-system finding.
Prioritize the equipment alarm as evidence of an isolated device fault.
Prioritize the physiologic change and exclude equipment from the assessment.
Prioritize alarm suppression before investigating the patient or system.
questions.explanation: Insufflation can affect patient physiology; equipment and patient changes require integrated evaluation.
whyOthers: The concurrent clinical change requires patient assessment as well as equipment assessment.
The insufflation-system finding may contribute to the patient’s change.
Suppressing an alarm does not resolve its cause or the clinical finding.

questions.prompt: During the head-and-neck case, an ignition source is requested near supplemental oxygen. Each discipline assumes another has assessed fire risk. What must be established?
options: A shared oxidizer, fuel, and ignition plan.
Independent discipline-specific assumptions without a team discussion.
Only confirmation that the energy generator self-test passed.
Only availability of a fire extinguisher outside the room.
questions.explanation: Fire prevention requires a common plan at the point where the elements coincide; separate assumptions can leave a gap.
whyOthers: Responsibility ambiguity is the scenario's central hazard.
Generator function does not assess the whole fire triangle.
Response resources do not replace prevention.

questions.prompt: A patient has an implanted electronic device, and monopolar energy is planned. What makes a generic 'implant present' note insufficient?
options: The particular implant requires coordinated energy and monitoring assessment.
The return electrode’s satisfactory contact establishes implant compatibility.
The generator’s satisfactory self-test establishes implant compatibility.
The last patient’s successful energy use establishes implant compatibility.
questions.explanation: Implanted devices differ, and energy strategy needs patient- and device-specific team planning.
whyOthers: Return-electrode contact addresses one risk; it does not resolve implant-specific interference planning.
Generator function does not establish the particular implant’s perioperative management.
Another patient’s implant and procedural circumstances may differ.

questions.prompt: A laser fibre's tip is damaged, but its connection fits and the system powers on. What should determine clinical use?
options: Resolve the damaged tip before activating the laser fibre clinically.
Use a successful connection check to clear the fibre for activation.
Use a reduced power setting to compensate for the damaged tip.
Use a brief patient-tissue activation to assess output quality.
questions.explanation: A damaged delivery component can alter energy output; connection and power-on do not establish safe function.
whyOthers: Mechanical connection does not establish the integrity of energy delivery.
Lower output does not validate a damaged component as safe.
Patient use is not an acceptable substitute for resolving a known integrity defect.

questions.prompt: The plume unit loses effective suction while energy use continues. A respirator is available. What is the best control response?
options: Restore effective source capture with the team.
Continue unchanged because the respirator restores source control.
Move the unit farther away to reduce noise.
Change only the generator power while leaving capture ineffective.
questions.explanation: Plume protection depends on functioning near-source evacuation; PPE does not repair its loss.
whyOthers: Respiratory protection and source capture serve different functions.
Distance can further impair capture.
Power adjustment alone does not restore evacuation.

questions.prompt: During a mobile imaging exposure, an unprotected staff member is called toward the table for a nonurgent task. What is the safest coordination?
options: Avoid unnecessary exposure using planned communication and protection.
Ask the staff member to approach quickly before the image completes.
Assume the sterile gown supplies the needed radiation protection.
Let each person decide independently when the beam is active.
questions.explanation: Exposure communication lets staff avoid unnecessary irradiation while maintaining appropriate protection for required presence.
whyOthers: Brief unnecessary proximity still increases avoidable exposure.
A surgical gown is not the specified radiation shield.
Shared timing information is part of the safety process.

questions.prompt: A critical monitor reports a sudden implausible change while the patient also has subtle new signs. What is the best first approach?
options: Assess the patient and verify the reported measurement together.
Use the unusual displayed value to exclude a real physiologic change.
Use the new clinical signs to accept the displayed number without verification.
Use absence of a second alarm to defer both assessments.
questions.explanation: An artifact and a real patient change can coexist; integrated assessment avoids both blind acceptance and premature dismissal.
whyOthers: An implausible value can be erroneous, but the concurrent signs still require clinical assessment.
Signs support assessment but do not validate a potentially faulty measurement.
One concerning reading with new signs warrants assessment before another alarm.

questions.prompt: A specimen's collected laterality differs from a preprinted label. The patient identifiers are correct. What is the best action?
options: Reconcile and correct the actual site label.
Send it because correct patient identity is enough.
Keep the preprinted side because it matches the booking.
Ask pathology to correct laterality after examining the tissue.
questions.explanation: Specimen accuracy includes the actual site and laterality as well as the patient; booking information may not reflect collection.
whyOthers: Identity does not remove site-specific diagnostic error.
Preprinted information must be checked against the actual event.
Tissue appearance may not establish laterality.

questions.prompt: A nurse assigned to continuous sedation monitoring is asked to fetch a nonurgent specimen container from outside. No qualified replacement is present. What is the best response?
options: Maintain dedicated monitoring and delegate container retrieval.
Leave briefly because the patient was stable at the last check.
Delegate monitoring to any available observer.
Use an audible monitor alarm as a substitute for the assigned nurse.
questions.explanation: The sedation-monitoring nurse performs those duties continuously; other requests must not create an unmonitored interval.
whyOthers: A previous stable observation does not assure continued stability.
Replacement needs appropriate capability and authorization.
Alarms do not replace continuous clinical monitoring and response.

questions.prompt: A plume-producing procedure uses an evacuation strategy framed only as staff protection. What patient-safety consideration supports source control too?
options: The patient can also be exposed to plume within the surgical environment.
Sterile draping is the primary control for the patient’s airborne plume exposure.
A functioning room ventilation system eliminates the patient’s source exposure.
Absence of an immediate patient symptom establishes adequate plume control.
questions.explanation: Plume management protects patients and personnel; sterile barriers do not remove airborne or chemical exposure.
whyOthers: A drape is not an airborne plume-control system.
General dilution ventilation does not replace capture near the source.
Symptoms are not a reliable endpoint for deciding whether source control is needed.

questions.prompt: A new device cannot function without proprietary single-use accessories. The capital purchase is funded, but supply continuity is unresolved. What should be established before adoption?
options: Establish reliable compatible consumables throughout the device’s expected use.
Use the funded capital purchase as evidence the complete pathway is viable.
Use one trial accessory as evidence future compatible stock is available.
Use the warranty as evidence proprietary accessories will remain accessible.
questions.explanation: Equipment availability depends on its recurring consumables, storage, costs, and support rather than the capital item alone.
whyOthers: Capital funding does not establish the ongoing supplies required to use the device.
A sample does not demonstrate sustainable compatible supply.
Warranty coverage does not by itself establish accessory availability.

questions.prompt: Maintenance identifies a fault in a needed device, and a repaired alternative is available without a completed return-to-use check. What is the best resource decision?
options: Establish a checked, functional alternative with a competent operator.
Use the repair completion record as the alternative’s return-to-use check.
Use the alternative’s compatible indication as its functional readiness check.
Use the current operator’s old-model experience as the replacement’s readiness check.
questions.explanation: A safe substitution needs verified readiness; choosing between two unverified devices does not resolve the finding.
whyOthers: A repair record does not replace the required verification of readiness after repair.
Appropriate intended use does not demonstrate actual function.
Experience with another model does not establish device function or replacement-specific competence.

questions.prompt: A unit's throughput proposal removes protected perioperative education and evidence review to fund faster turnover. Its authors say output is the best proxy for ORNAC's mission. Which counterproposal most directly preserves that mission?
options: Preserve evidence-informed education while evaluating safe improvements in throughput.
Preserve turnover targets while shifting all practice learning to vendor demonstrations.
Preserve procedure volume while using current routines as the sole practice benchmark.
Preserve budget targets while evaluating success only by completed case numbers.
questions.explanation: ORNAC's mission links safe surgery with perioperative education and evidence-based practice. Operational output alone does not demonstrate that these foundations have been preserved.
whyOthers: Vendor demonstrations may contribute to learning but do not replace evidence-informed perioperative education.
Current routines alone do not establish evidence-informed safe practice.
Budget and case numbers do not measure the mission’s safety, education, and evidence components.

questions.prompt: A committee is choosing a long-term perioperative development strategy. All proposals include education, but only one explicitly connects collaboration, evaluated best-practice adoption, and excellence in patient care. Which proposal most closely advances ORNAC's vision?
options: Develop practice collaboratively, adopt evaluated evidence, and monitor patient-care improvement.
Standardize existing routines, reward attendance, and monitor document completion.
Expand individual courses, preserve existing routines, and monitor procedure volume.
Purchase new technology, increase course attendance, and monitor acquisition targets.
questions.explanation: The vision links collaborative professional advancement, continuing development, evidence-based best practices, and excellent surgical patient care.
whyOthers: Consistency and attendance alone do not establish evaluated best-practice adoption or patient-care improvement.
Individual education and volume omit the collaborative and evaluated practice-development components.
New technology and acquisition totals do not establish evidence-based adoption or excellent patient-care outcomes.

questions.prompt: Before the first case, sterile setup has been opened when the nurse notices the preliminary damp-dusting was not done. Terminal cleaning was documented the previous night. Which assessment best explains why the missing step still matters?
options: Preliminary cleaning addresses contamination accumulated after terminal cleaning and precedes setup.
Terminal cleaning establishes room cleanliness until the first patient enters.
Sterile packaging establishes cleanliness of the surrounding room surfaces.
Preliminary cleaning is a response to known infection rather than routine readiness.
questions.explanation: Preliminary inspection and damp-dusting prepare the room before supplies and patients enter; documented terminal cleaning does not eliminate subsequently accumulated contamination.
whyOthers: Dust and contamination may accumulate after terminal cleaning.
Package processing does not clean the environment around an opened field.
Preliminary room preparation applies routinely, not only for known infection.

questions.prompt: A nurse is competent in a procedure and the organizational role permits it, but regulated authority for the activity has not been established. What is the controlling next step?
options: Verify the applicable regulatory authorization before independent performance.
Proceed because competence replaces regulated scope.
Proceed because local policy can independently override legislation.
Use the guideline's technical instructions as legal authorization.
questions.explanation: Scope, organizational role, practice guidance, and competence are distinct; all applicable conditions must be satisfied.
whyOthers: Ability does not grant legal permission.
Local policy does not independently displace regulated requirements.
A technical guideline is not a grant of regulated scope.

questions.prompt: A closed femoral fracture is internally fixed. There is no infection or inflammation, no entry into a respiratory, urinary, genital, or alimentary tract, and no sterile breach. The incision is primarily closed. Which final wound class applies?
options: Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class III: contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: This is Class I. Inserting an implant does not itself make a wound contaminated; classify the actual tissue and intraoperative conditions.
whyOthers: Class II requires controlled entry into one of the specified tracts; implant placement is not tract entry.
There is no fresh open injury, major sterile breach, GI spillage, or nonpurulent inflammation to support Class III.
There is no established infection, old traumatic wound, or perforated viscus to support Class IV.

questions.prompt: During an elective colectomy, the colon is opened under controlled conditions without spillage, prior infection, or a break in sterility. Which final wound class applies?
options: Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class I: clean.
Class III: contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: Controlled entry into the alimentary tract without infection or an aseptic breach is Class II, even when the operation proceeds without complications.
whyOthers: Class I excludes entry into the alimentary tract, so an uncomplicated colectomy is not automatically clean.
Controlled tract entry alone does not establish Class III; the stated contamination or inflammatory conditions are absent.
There is no existing infection or perforated viscus to make this Class IV.

questions.prompt: An otherwise uninfected patient undergoes debridement of a fresh open accidental forearm wound. There is no old injury, pus, or perforated viscus. Which wound class best matches the findings?
options: Class III: contaminated.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: A fresh open accidental wound fits Class III. The distinction is the fresh exposure, rather than an assumption that all traumatic wounds are already infected.
whyOthers: The wound is already open from an accidental injury; absence of infection does not make it a clean operative wound.
Class II describes controlled tract entry and does not describe this fresh accidental wound.
Class IV includes old traumatic wounds or established infection; neither is described here.

questions.prompt: Laparotomy reveals a perforated sigmoid colon with established fecal peritonitis before operative manipulation. Which final wound class applies?
options: Class IV: dirty or infected.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class III: contaminated.
questions.explanation: A perforated viscus and existing clinical infection support Class IV. This differs from contamination newly introduced by intraoperative GI spillage.
whyOthers: Pre-existing perforation and infection exclude Class I.
This is not controlled entry into an uninfected tract, as required for Class II.
Class III describes contamination such as operative spillage; the pre-existing perforated viscus and infection here support Class IV.

questions.prompt: A colectomy begins with controlled entry into an uninfected colon. Later, a substantial amount of bowel contents spills into the operative field. No pre-existing perforation or clinical infection is found. Which final wound class should be confirmed?
options: Class III: contaminated.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: GI spillage changes the findings to Class III. The final classification reflects what occurred, rather than the original planned Class II operation.
whyOthers: The alimentary tract was entered and spillage occurred, excluding a clean wound.
The case no longer meets the controlled, uncontaminated conditions supporting Class II.
Operative spillage alone is not the same as pre-existing infection or a perforated viscus supporting Class IV.

questions.prompt: An operative incision encounters acute inflammation without pus. There is no established clinical infection, old traumatic injury, or perforated viscus. Which ORNAC wound class best fits this stated finding?
options: Class III: contaminated.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: ORNAC lists nonpurulent inflammation under Class III. Do not infer Class IV solely from inflammation when the case explicitly excludes clinical infection.
whyOthers: Inflammation is inconsistent with the clean conditions described for Class I.
Class II is controlled tract entry without prior infection; it does not account for this nonpurulent inflammatory finding.
The stem excludes established clinical infection, pus, old trauma, and perforated viscera; nonpurulent inflammation is listed under Class III.

questions.prompt: A patient presents several days after a penetrating injury. Surgery addresses an old traumatic wound containing devitalized tissue. Which wound class is appropriate even if the operative field has no obvious pus?
options: Class IV: dirty or infected.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class III: contaminated.
questions.explanation: An old traumatic wound supports Class IV. Visible pus is not required for every Class IV wound; the injury history and operative findings matter.
whyOthers: An old traumatic wound with devitalized tissue does not meet clean-wound criteria.
There is no controlled tract-entry scenario supporting Class II.
The distinction from Class III is an old traumatic wound rather than a fresh open accidental wound.

questions.prompt: A clean operation is booked, but a major break in sterile technique occurs before closure. No tract was entered, and no pre-existing infection is identified. After the breach is managed, which final wound class best reflects the event?
options: Class III: contaminated.
Class I: clean.
Class II: clean-contaminated.
Class IV: dirty or infected.
questions.explanation: A major break in sterility supports Class III. Managing the breach is essential but does not erase the event from the final wound-class assessment.
whyOthers: The major sterile breach prevents assigning Class I solely from the original booking or corrective action.
Class II is controlled tract entry without a sterile breach; that does not describe this case.
There is no old trauma, established clinical infection, or perforated viscus to support Class IV.

questions.prompt: An urgent surgical patient has symptoms strongly suspicious for infectious pulmonary tuberculosis; confirmation is pending. Which additional-precaution category should guide the initial pathway?
options: Airborne precautions while the suspected infectious risk is assessed.
Droplet precautions only until a sputum result is positive.
Contact precautions only because respiratory secretions contaminate surfaces.
Routine practices only unless an aerosol-generating procedure is scheduled.
questions.explanation: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB warrants an airborne pathway without waiting for confirmation. Routine practices continue, and IPAC helps plan the room, respiratory protection, transport, and airway procedures.
whyOthers: Waiting for a positive test delays control of a suspected airborne risk; a droplet-only plan is insufficient.
Surface contamination does not eliminate the airborne route of infectious pulmonary TB.
Airborne precautions are not limited to the time an aerosol-generating procedure is performed.

questions.prompt: Two patients have rash illnesses: one has suspected rubeola and the other rubella. Which distinction matches ORNAC’s named additional-precaution categories?
options: Rubeola is listed under airborne; rubella is listed under droplet.
Both are listed under droplet because both cause a rash.
Rubeola is listed under droplet; rubella is listed under airborne.
Both are listed under contact because neither diagnosis concerns an airway.
questions.explanation: Rubeola means measles and is an airborne example; rubella is a different infection and is a droplet example. Similar names and rash presentations do not imply the same transmission plan.
whyOthers: Rubeola is an airborne example, so assigning both illnesses to droplet misses a clinically important distinction.
This reverses the guideline’s categories for these two different diseases.
The presence of a rash does not exclude respiratory transmission or make contact the category for both.

questions.prompt: A patient with active chickenpox has vesicular lesions and needs urgent surgery. Which combination accounts for both recognized transmission routes, using ORNAC’s airborne example and PHAC’s disease-specific table?
options: Airborne and contact precautions, in addition to routine practices.
Droplet precautions alone, in addition to routine practices.
Contact precautions alone once visible lesions are covered.
Airborne precautions alone, with contact measures unnecessary.
questions.explanation: Varicella requires airborne and contact precautions. ORNAC identifies its airborne risk; PHAC also identifies contact transmission from lesions. Covering lesions does not remove the airborne requirement.
whyOthers: Droplet alone does not address the specified airborne and contact routes.
Covering lesions does not eliminate the airborne route.
Airborne measures do not replace the contact component.

additionalReferences.name: PHAC: Routine Practices and Additional Precautions, Table 5 — varicella

questions.prompt: For a patient with seasonal influenza, which ORNAC §2.2 named category specifically addresses the usual close-range respiratory exposure, before considering extra measures required by local policy or an airway procedure?
options: Droplet precautions.
Airborne precautions as the only listed influenza category.
Contact precautions as the only listed influenza category.
Routine practices without any additional category.
questions.explanation: ORNAC lists influenza among droplet examples. This identifies the listed respiratory category, not a complete patient-specific isolation plan; other measures and aerosol-generating procedures require assessment.
whyOthers: ORNAC’s named influenza example appears in its droplet list; procedure-specific airborne controls are a separate assessment.
Contact measures may be relevant to the care plan, but they are not the named respiratory category being tested here.
Influenza is explicitly an additional-precaution example, so routine practices alone do not answer this question.

questions.prompt: An adolescent with suspected pertussis is being assessed before a procedure; no aerosol-generating intervention is underway. Which named ORNAC category most directly matches this infection?
options: Droplet precautions, with routine practices and task-specific PPE.
Airborne precautions because every prolonged cough is an airborne diagnosis.
Contact precautions alone because secretions are present.
Routine practices alone until antibiotic treatment is complete.
questions.explanation: Pertussis is an ORNAC droplet example. The infection and anticipated tasks guide additional measures; the length of a cough does not by itself assign an airborne diagnosis.
whyOthers: A prolonged cough is not itself the criterion for changing pertussis from the listed droplet category to airborne.
Contact precautions alone omit the listed droplet category for pertussis.
Suspected transmission risk requires precautions now, rather than waiting through treatment.

questions.prompt: A colleague groups mumps, rubella, and measles together as droplet examples. Which correction most accurately matches ORNAC’s lists?
options: Keep mumps and rubella under droplet; move measles to airborne.
Keep rubella and measles under droplet; move mumps to contact.
Keep mumps under droplet; move rubella and measles to contact.
Move all three to airborne because they are vaccine-preventable.
questions.explanation: Mumps and rubella are listed droplet examples; measles, also called rubeola, is an airborne example. Vaccine preventability does not determine the transmission category.
whyOthers: Measles belongs in the airborne list, and mumps is listed under droplet rather than contact.
Rubella remains a droplet example and measles is airborne; contact is not the listed replacement for either.
Vaccination status and vaccine availability do not make every vaccine-preventable infection airborne.

questions.prompt: A surgical patient is colonized with MRSA but has no fever or active wound infection. Which interpretation best matches ORNAC’s contact-precaution framework?
options: Colonization can justify contact precautions; absence of symptomatic infection does not remove transmission risk.
Contact precautions begin only if MRSA enters the bloodstream.
MRSA colonization requires airborne precautions because an organism may be shed.
Routine practices alone are sufficient whenever the patient is afebrile.
questions.explanation: ORNAC’s contact framework includes suspected or known colonization as well as infection, and lists MRSA as an antibiotic-resistant organism example. Follow the organization’s IPAC protocol.
whyOthers: Bloodstream infection is not a prerequisite for contact precautions for a colonized patient.
Shedding does not make MRSA an airborne example; contact transfer is the relevant listed pathway.
Lack of fever does not establish that a colonized patient cannot transmit an organism.

questions.prompt: A patient’s record flags VRE colonization. The patient has no cough and the planned incision is clean. Which additional-precaution category is relevant independently of the wound class?
options: Contact precautions according to the IPAC plan.
Droplet precautions because resistance implies respiratory spread.
Airborne precautions because VRE is an antibiotic-resistant organism.
No additional precautions because the procedure is Class I.
questions.explanation: VRE is a listed contact example. Wound classification describes the operative field; it does not decide whether a patient needs transmission precautions.
whyOthers: Antibiotic resistance does not establish droplet transmission.
VRE’s resistance does not change its listed contact category to airborne.
A clean operative wound does not negate patient colonization or its contact pathway.

questions.prompt: A patient awaiting urgent surgery has suspected C. difficile-associated diarrhea. Which core additional category addresses the relevant exposure pathway while diagnostic results are pending?
options: Contact precautions alongside routine practices.
Droplet precautions only because stool testing is pending.
Airborne precautions only because environmental persistence implies airborne spread.
Routine practices only unless the surgical wound is contaminated.
questions.explanation: C. difficile is an ORNAC contact example. Suspected infection is enough to plan precautions; the patient’s enteric risk and the operation’s wound class are separate assessments.
whyOthers: Pending stool results do not change the suspected enteric organism to a droplet example.
Environmental persistence does not itself establish an airborne route.
Transmission precautions are not conditional on assigning a contaminated surgical wound class.

questions.prompt: A patient with suspected norovirus gastroenteritis needs an urgent procedure and vomits during assessment. Which plan best distinguishes the core category from exposure-specific protection?
options: Use contact precautions and add PPE for the assessed splash or respiratory exposure during vomiting.
Use airborne precautions for every norovirus encounter because vomiting occurs.
Use droplet precautions alone and omit contact controls after vomiting stops.
Use routine practices alone once the patient receives an antiemetic.
questions.explanation: ORNAC lists norovirus gastroenteritis under contact precautions. Vomiting also requires a point-of-care exposure assessment and appropriate PPE; symptom treatment does not establish that transmission risk has ended.
whyOthers: Vomiting calls for exposure-specific assessment but does not make every norovirus encounter an airborne-category case.
Droplet measures alone omit the listed contact pathway, including contaminated hands and surfaces.
An antiemetic can reduce symptoms without eliminating the infectious contact risk.

questions.prompt: A patient has suspected scabies and an IPAC-directed contact plan. A nurse proposes replacing it with a respirator-only plan because the patient’s skin appears dry. Which reasoning is best?
options: Scabies is listed under contact; skin appearance does not replace the prescribed contact measures with airborne controls.
Dry skin means routine practices alone are sufficient while confirmation is pending.
All skin infestations require airborne precautions whenever the patient moves.
A respirator alone provides the same transmission protection as gloves and a gown for the relevant contact.
questions.explanation: ORNAC lists scabies as a contact example. Apply the IPAC plan and barriers appropriate to patient and surface contact; the appearance of the skin does not reassign the route.
whyOthers: Dry appearance does not rule out the suspected infestation or its contact risk.
Movement does not establish an airborne category for every skin infestation.
Respiratory protection does not substitute for barriers needed for the assessed contact exposure.

questions.prompt: A child with RSV is scheduled for urgent surgery. RSV appears in both ORNAC’s droplet and contact example lists. Which plan best reflects that overlap?
options: Address both droplet and contact pathways rather than treating the categories as mutually exclusive.
Select airborne alone because an organism cannot belong to two categories.
Select droplet alone because respiratory symptoms exclude contact transmission.
Select contact alone because contaminated equipment excludes respiratory transmission.
questions.explanation: ORNAC lists RSV in both categories. A care plan can combine additional precautions, with routine practices continuing and airway-procedure risks assessed separately.
whyOthers: An organism can require combined measures; membership in two lists does not itself indicate airborne transmission.
Respiratory symptoms do not eliminate transfer by hands or contaminated equipment.
Contact transmission does not eliminate the listed droplet pathway.

questions.prompt: An ultrasound probe is normally used on intact skin but will now enter a sterile operative cavity. Which reprocessing decision follows its intended contact rather than its usual equipment name?
options: Treat this application as critical and use validated cleaning followed by sterilization.
Keep it noncritical because most previous examinations involved intact skin.
Treat it as semicritical and use high-level disinfection as the sole endpoint.
Leave its class unchanged if a disposable barrier is added.
questions.explanation: Spaulding classification follows the contact in the intended application. Entry into a sterile cavity is critical, requiring validated sterilization; a cover does not by itself downgrade that requirement.
whyOthers: Prior intact-skin use does not determine the class for a new sterile-cavity application.
High-level disinfection alone is not the endpoint for a critical device entering a sterile cavity.
A barrier does not automatically change critical tissue contact into a noncritical application.

questions.prompt: A flexible gastroscope will contact GI mucosa without penetrating sterile tissue. After validated cleaning, what is the minimum acceptable Spaulding endpoint when the device instructions support it?
options: High-level disinfection for a semicritical device.
Low-level disinfection because the GI tract is not sterile.
No disinfection because visible soil has been removed.
Critical classification solely because the scope is inserted into the body.
questions.explanation: Mucosal contact without penetration of sterile tissue is semicritical. ORNAC describes sterilization as ideal and high-level disinfection as an acceptable minimum for suitable semicritical devices.
whyOthers: A nonsterile mucosal surface still requires the semicritical level, not the noncritical low-level endpoint.
Cleaning is necessary but does not replace the required disinfection or sterilization step.
Insertion into the body alone does not define critical status; the contacted tissue and penetration matter.

questions.prompt: A reusable biopsy needle guide will contact sterile tissue during an image-guided biopsy. The team proposes a sterile cover and high-level disinfection. Which assessment is most accurate?
options: The guide’s critical application requires validated sterilization; a cover does not justify substituting high-level disinfection.
The cover changes the guide to noncritical, so low-level disinfection is enough.
Any ultrasound accessory is semicritical regardless of tissue contact.
High-level disinfection and sterilization are interchangeable endpoints for critical devices.
questions.explanation: The critical contact, not the accessory’s name or the presence of a cover, establishes the required sterilization endpoint. Verify the intended use and validated device instructions.
whyOthers: A cover is not a general authorization to downgrade a device contacting sterile tissue to noncritical.
An accessory’s association with ultrasound does not override its actual tissue contact.
High-level disinfection does not substitute for required sterilization of a critical device.

questions.prompt: Reusable ECG leads contact intact skin only but are visibly soiled with blood after handling. Which interpretation separates classification from cleaning needs?
options: They remain noncritical for this use, but need cleaning before the indicated compatible disinfection process.
Blood on the surface makes the leads critical even without contact with sterile tissue.
Visible blood makes all subsequent uses semicritical regardless of tissue contact.
Their noncritical class means the visible contamination can remain if disinfectant is sprayed over it.
questions.explanation: Spaulding class is based on intended tissue contact. Soil still must be removed and the blood-contamination protocol followed with a compatible product; being noncritical does not excuse inadequate cleaning.
whyOthers: Surface blood is a contamination problem to manage, not proof that the leads enter sterile tissue.
Semicritical classification depends on mucosal or nonintact-skin contact, not blood being found on a surface alone.
Disinfectant applied over retained soil does not replace the necessary cleaning step.

questions.prompt: A transvaginal ultrasound probe is used with an intact single-use cover. It contacts mucosa without entering sterile tissue. Which between-patient approach best fits Spaulding principles?
options: Clean and perform validated high-level disinfection at minimum; the cover does not remove the semicritical requirement.
Remove the cover and use low-level disinfection because the barrier appeared intact.
Reclassify it as critical solely because it entered a body opening.
Reuse it after changing the cover without cleaning or disinfection.
questions.explanation: Mucosal contact makes this application semicritical. A cover is an additional barrier, not a replacement for the validated between-patient reprocessing process.
whyOthers: An apparently intact cover does not authorize a lower endpoint for the semicritical probe.
A body opening is not synonymous with sterile tissue; mucosal contact without penetration is semicritical.
Changing a cover does not replace cleaning and the required reprocessing endpoint.

questions.prompt: A reusable heat-sensitive instrument must enter sterile tissue, but cannot tolerate the available steam cycle. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Arrange an appropriate validated sterilization method or a suitable sterile alternative before use.
Use high-level disinfection because heat sensitivity changes the instrument to semicritical.
Use low-level disinfection if the instrument is covered with a sterile sleeve.
Run the incompatible steam cycle because critical classification overrides the manufacturer’s instructions.
questions.explanation: Critical tissue contact still requires sterilization. Heat sensitivity changes which validated method or alternative is suitable, not the required microbiological endpoint.
whyOthers: Heat sensitivity does not change the intended tissue contact or permit a critical device to receive only high-level disinfection.
A sterile sleeve does not establish that low-level disinfection is sufficient for critical use.
An incompatible cycle risks damage or ineffective processing; classification does not authorize ignoring validated instructions.

questions.prompt: Donna is performing an initial count with the scrub nurse. What items does she need to count?
options: Sponges, sharps and miscellaneous items
Sharps and miscellaneous items
Sponges, sharps, instruments and miscellaneous items
Sponges, sharps and instruments
questions.explanation: An initial surgical count accounts for sponges, sharps, instruments, and miscellaneous countable items; minimally invasive access does not remove retained-item risk.
optionExplanations: Omits instruments, which the review includes because a laparoscopic procedure may convert to an open operation.
Omits sponges and instruments.
Includes all four count categories.
Omits miscellaneous countable items.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: When setting up the table, the scrub nurse states that she does not need a needle counter for the laparoscopic appendectomy; she only has one needle and one blade on the table. What should the circulating nurse do?
options: Agree with her because cost containment is important.
Give her a needle counter and remind her that safety is for all staff.
Tell the scrub nurse that she will give her one if the case becomes more involved.
Agree because a needle counter is not necessary for only two sharps.
questions.explanation: Contain and track sharps safely even when only a few are used. A small case still exposes personnel to a sharps injury.
optionExplanations: Cost containment cannot justify removing a safety control.
Provides safe sharps containment from the start.
Delays protection until after exposure has already occurred.
Two sharps still require safe containment and counting.

questions.prompt: When entering the abdomen with the trocar, the surgeon has difficulty getting through the peritoneum. Once inside and exploring with the laparoscope, the surgeon notices a perforation in the bowel, and there is leakage. What should the scrub nurse anticipate?
options: Bowel resection
Perforated appendix
Repair of perforated bowel
Gastric ulcer perforation
questions.explanation: The observed problem is an iatrogenic bowel perforation. Prepare for repair and possible conversion to open surgery; resection depends on the extent of injury.
optionExplanations: Resection may be needed for a major injury, but is not established by this description.
The visible injury occurred during trocar entry rather than being described as appendiceal perforation.
Directly addresses the observed bowel injury.
No gastric injury is described.

questions.prompt: The surgical procedure was completed faster than anticipated by the anesthesia provider and Nina is not reversing from the non-depolarizing muscle relaxants given. Which drug is the anesthesia provider likely to give?
options: Succinylcholine chloride (Anectine)
Propofol (Diprivan)
Rocuronium bromide (Zemuron)
Neostigmine bromide (Prostigmin)
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is the listed drug used to reverse suitable nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade. The other choices cause neuromuscular blockade or provide hypnosis rather than reverse paralysis. Monitoring and the prescribed reversal regimen still apply.
optionExplanations: Produces depolarizing neuromuscular blockade rather than reversing it.
Provides hypnosis; it does not reverse paralysis.
Is itself a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker.
The drug class fits reversal, with formulation, monitoring, and antimuscarinic precautions verified.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.currentGuidance: The recorded option names neostigmine bromide. IV reversal uses the prescribed injectable formulation, commonly neostigmine methylsulfate; salts and routes are not interchangeable. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and the prescribed antimuscarinic remain important.

questions.prompt: Following extubation, Nina’s airway becomes irritated and she shows signs of laryngospasm. What should the circulating nurse anticipate as an initial measure?
options: Administration of succinylcholine chloride (Anectine)
Use a reversal agent for the non-depolarizing muscle relaxant
Provide 100% oxygen using positive pressure delivery
Putting Nina back into an anesthetized state
questions.explanation: Support oxygenation immediately with 100% oxygen, a tight mask, appropriate positive pressure, and jaw thrust while the anesthesia provider removes the stimulus. Persistent spasm may require deepening anesthesia or neuromuscular blockade.
optionExplanations: Can be needed for persistent spasm, but oxygenation measures come first.
Residual paralysis and laryngospasm are different problems.
Addresses the immediate oxygenation problem.
Not the review's initial measure. Anesthesia-led deepening of anesthesia may be part of escalation; it is not a substitute for initial oxygenation and airway maneuvers.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse is transferring Nina to the post-anesthesia care unit. What priorities should be included in the report to the recovery nurse?
options: Drains, Foley catheter, dressing applied
Age, weight, diagnosis, allergies
Allergies, operative procedure performed, laryngospasm
Allergies, location of mother, dressing applied
questions.explanation: Handoff must include the procedure, allergies, and the airway complication so PACU can anticipate recurrent obstruction or other respiratory concerns.
optionExplanations: Useful device and wound details, but omits the described airway event.
Basic assessment details, but omits the significant intraoperative complication.
Conveys the critical event and relevant operative history.
Family location and dressing details do not replace the airway handoff.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: What are the most important things for the circulating nurse to do when she meets Mrs. Snider in the holding area?
options: Confirm the patient's name using a minimum of two patient unique identifiers, confirm consent, and surgical site with patient.
Acknowledge the patient, confirm patient identity with the chart and documents and confirm surgical site accuracy.
Review history and physical examination, confirm consent and check blood results.
Ensure jewellery is removed, check patient health record and confirm n.p.o. status.
questions.explanation: Verify two patient identifiers and reconcile consent, planned procedure, and site with the patient whenever possible before proceeding.
optionExplanations: Includes the essential identity, consent, and site checks.
Does not explicitly reconcile consent with the patient using two identifiers.
Important assessment information, but identity and site verification are still required.
These preparations do not establish the correct patient, consent, and site.

origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: After Mrs. Snider is positioned and prepped, the scrub nurse is setting up and notices a small tear in the back table cover drape. What should the scrub nurse do?
options: Inform the circulating nurse, dismantle the set-up and order new supplies.
Use a sterile, impervious drape to cover the hole.
Continue with the set-up because Mrs. Snider is already asleep.
Tell the circulating nurse to document the break in technique.
questions.explanation: The recorded review treats the torn table drape as a contaminated setup. Inform the circulating nurse and replace the compromised setup promptly; documentation follows corrective action.
optionExplanations: Corrects the barrier breach immediately and communicates the need for replacement supplies.
The review considers the setup contaminated; covering the hole does not restore contaminated supplies to sterility.
An anesthetized patient does not justify continuing with a compromised sterile field.
Documentation is necessary, but corrective action comes first.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.currentGuidance: The key assumes the tear compromises the working sterile field. ORNAC requires recognition and correction of aseptic breaches. Assess the location and affected items, and replace contaminated supplies; simply placing a cover over contamination does not make it sterile.

questions.prompt: As the surgery progresses, the scrub nurse notices that the incision is larger and more tissue is being dissected than in other segmental resections she has been involved in before. What would be the scrub nurse’s responsibility to the patient?
options: Comment to the surgeon on the extent of the incision.
Bring her concerns to the attention of the circulating nurse.
Ask to see the consent form.
Assume the surgeon knows what he is doing and say nothing.
questions.explanation: The scrub nurse should raise the concern directly with the surgeon on the patient's behalf. The review tests active patient advocacy and clarification of the extent of surgery, rather than silently accepting an unexpected finding.
optionExplanations: Directly seeks clarification from the surgeon while advocating for the patient.
Involving the circulating nurse can help, but this option delays the direct clarification the review expects from the scrub nurse.
Consent should already have been checked; retrieving it alone does not address the surgeon's unexpected dissection.
Silence leaves the concern unresolved and does not advocate for the patient.

origin.name: CNA Practice Test — Perioperative (Meazure Learning recording)
origin.answerStatus: Correct option verified in the recorded exam review

questions.prompt: While Mrs. Snider’s surgery is in progress, several members of the nursing staff visit the operating room to give their best wishes. Since she was already asleep, most hung around the room conversing with the staff and checking periodically on the progress of the surgery. How should the circulating nurse respond to these visitors?
options: Allow only close friends in the operating room.
Send all visitors out of the operating room.
Call the supervisor to restrict traffic flow.
Put a “Closed Room” sign on the door.
questions.explanation: Restrict unnecessary OR traffic and protect the patient's privacy. Staff friendship does not make a social visit part of patient care.

questions.prompt: Mr. Potter, 20 years old, is on his way to the operating room from the Emergency Department with a gunshot wound to his chest. The Emergency Department report indicates the following: T 35 °C, HR 90, RR 16 and BP 118/70. Which of the following items are most appropriate in preparing the operating room for Mr. Potter's arrival?
options: Blood warmer, warm air thermoregulatory device and warm IV solutions
Antiembolism stockings, temperature probe and disposable drapes
Warm water, adequate supply of pressure dressings and heating lamp
Positioning aids, electrosurgical unit and cardiac arrest cart
questions.explanation: A temperature of 35 °C warrants active hypothermia management. Prepare approved warming devices, warmed IV fluids, and blood warming when transfusion is indicated, while the team treats the chest injury.
optionExplanations: Provides the targeted warming resources.
Does not directly correct the identified hypothermia.
Uncontrolled heating methods risk injury and do not provide the validated warming plan.
Important general equipment, but omits targeted temperature management.

questions.prompt: What is the best illustration of a perioperative nurse exemplifying cost consciousness?
options: A resource nurse who coordinates the custom packs to contain standardized items
A materials coordinator who purchases surgical items based on the lowest price
A circulating nurse who opens all sterile disposable items before the start of surgery
A scrub nurse who utilizes a suture towel instead of a disposable suture book
questions.explanation: Standardized, appropriately designed packs can reduce unnecessary items, variation, and waste while preserving clinical requirements. Lowest price alone is not a sound procurement criterion.
optionExplanations: Combines standardization with reduction of unnecessary resource use.
Ignores quality, compatibility, reprocessing, and total life-cycle cost.
Creates waste when items are not needed.
A towel is not automatically an approved safe sharps-management substitute.

questions.prompt: The perioperative nurse observes a blistered area over the elbow of Mrs. Clarke as she is being transferred postoperatively. This was not observed preoperatively. What should the nurse do?
options: Complete an incident report and document the observation on the operating room record.
Ignore the observation because this is a common occurrence.
Document the observation on the operating room record.
Complete and document the incident report on the operating room record.
questions.explanation: Assess and treat the new skin injury, document the clinical findings, communicate them at handoff, and file the separate safety report. Do not put the incident report itself into the patient record.
optionExplanations: Provides both clinical documentation and organizational safety reporting.
A new injury requires assessment rather than dismissal.
Clinical documentation alone omits the safety-reporting process.
Document clinical observations in the record, not the incident report itself.

questions.prompt: Ms. Vlasek, 83 years old, is scheduled for a total hip arthroplasty. The perioperative nurse informs the surgeon that the stem size most likely required is not available in the hospital. The nurse has been informed that the implant should arrive at the hospital in about 2½ hours. What is the nurse’s best course of action?
options: Proceed with the case because the implant will be available in time for use.
Start the case when it is confirmed that the implant has arrived at the hospital.
Confirm with the surgeon that an implant has been sent and then start the case.
Confirm with the supplier that the implant is on its way and then proceed with the case.
questions.explanation: Do not begin on the assumption that a required implant will arrive in time. Confirm actual receipt, correct size, sterility or completed processing, and readiness with the team before proceeding.
optionExplanations: Estimated delivery time is not verified implant readiness.
Is the safest listed choice, with readiness and processing checks in addition to arrival.
Dispatch does not establish arrival or readiness.
A supplier's assurance that it is en route does not establish availability for use.

cases.CASE01: An adult is scheduled for a left knee procedure. During preparation, the team checks the record, consent, site mark, and planned time-out.
cases.CASE02: An adult is preparing for major abdominal surgery. The team reviews allergies, infection prevention, temperature management, and clot risk.
cases.CASE03: An anesthetized patient is transferred and positioned for a prolonged prone procedure. Skin, pressure, nerve, and handoff risks are considered.
cases.CASE04: During an open abdominal procedure, sponges are used and the closing count does not reconcile. The team must prevent an unintentionally retained item.
cases.CASE05: During surgery, a verbal order is given and specimens are sent for time-sensitive analysis. Several clear solutions are on the field.
cases.CASE06: Before anesthesia, a family history raises concern for malignant hyperthermia. The team reviews preparedness and recognition of a possible crisis.
cases.CASE07: A robotic minimally invasive operation is planned with some staff new to the platform. The team reviews docking, emergency access, and plume controls.
cases.CASE08: An urgent operation is needed for a patient with suspected respiratory infection. Airway management and subsequent room turnover require planning.
cases.CASE09: A joint replacement is scheduled. A loaned tray and implant arrive, and the team assesses validated processing and load release before use.
cases.CASE10: A head and neck procedure uses oxygen and surgical energy after skin preparation. The team is concerned about fire prevention and safe electrode handling.
cases.CASE11: An extremity operation requires a pneumatic tourniquet. The patient has fragile skin, and equipment function and inflation time need attention.
cases.CASE12: A severely injured patient is treated in the OR, with possible medicolegal evidence. The team plans preservation and, if death occurs, appropriate handling.
cases.CASE13: A pandemic surge affects an urgent surgical service. Patient routing, personnel communication, and protective-equipment supply are under review.
cases.CASE14: An OR is reviewing equipment reliability after a recall and an intraoperative malfunction. Maintenance and a safe replacement are discussed.
cases.CASE15: A reprocessing team sorts different patient-care devices by Spaulding infection-risk class and prepares them for the appropriate validated process.
cases.REC-CASE-1: Donna, the circulating nurse, is admitting 16-year-old Nina to the operating room to have a laparoscopic appendectomy. Nina is allergic to shellfish, dust and recently reacted to penicillin.
cases.REC-CASE-2: Mrs. Snider, a 44-year-old perioperative nurse, is being admitted to her own facility for a segmental resection of her left breast. Since her breast biopsy 2 weeks ago, she has thoroughly discussed the options with her surgeon and is comfortable with their joint decision.
cases.REC-CASE-3: Mr. Samson, 67 years old, is having a resection of his transverse colon with colostomy. The perioperative nurses are completing the final count. The surgeon unscrubs and sprays the incision area with a waterproof aerosol dressing which also lands on the resident's gloves. The resident activates the electrosurgical pencil to cauterize a small bleeding vessel. Flames leap along the incision and across the resident's gloves.
cases.REC-CASE-4: Chad, 16 years old, is brought to the operating room suite for open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) of a fractured right femur and ORIF of his left arm sustained in a motor vehicle collision. Chad received pain medication in the Emergency Department just prior to transfer to the operating room. His parents have accompanied him to the operating room, and his mother states that Chad has an allergy to penicillin. Chad does not remember when he last had something to eat or drink.
cases.REC-CASE-5: At 18:00, Dr. Jamieson calls the operating room staff to inform them that Mr. Roberts, 64 years old, will be coming to the operating room within half an hour. He has suspected intra-abdominal injuries, facial trauma and a fractured femur.
